fixes.explanation: True, friend. David tells Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought it to him, and then "…David inquired of the LORD…" Once the ephod is there, David turns to the LORD with his questions.

True, friend. The text says, "And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day." That ruling was that the two groups "…will share alike." I think that's a rule worth keeping around.

Elders is right. The text says David sent some of the plunder "…to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying…" The message was, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies." The writer calls them his friends. I think that's a generous way to share.
Tore sounds like a natural word for a raid, but it isn't the one in the text. The verse says the Amalekites "…attacked Ziklag, and burned it down." Burned is the word the text uses.

Nobody mentions the Philistine army in this verse, friend. What the text says is that David was greatly distressed "…because the people spoke of stoning him…" The men are hurting over their sons and daughters, and that's what the talk is about. I think it was a heavy time in that camp.

Battle plans aren't what the text names, friend. It says, "But David found strength in the LORD his God." After that he asks for the ephod and inquires of the LORD. I'd say that's a good place to turn.

That sounds sensible, but it's not what the LORD says. David asks if he should pursue the raiders and if he'll overtake them. The LORD answers, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives." That's a go, friend, not a stay.

Two hundred is right. The text says "…two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook." That leaves David with four hundred to keep going. I bet exhaustion hits hard after that kind of heartbreak.

I can see why you'd think that, but the text goes another way. David's men find the Egyptian in the field and bring him to David. Then "They gave the man water to drink and food to eat…" That's what the text tells us they did for him.
Moabite isn't in this scene at all, friend. The man tells David, "I am an Egyptian," and says he is "…the slave of an Amalekite." So his master is an Amalekite. That's the answer for the blank.
It's not true, friend. The Egyptian says, "My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill." The reason he gives is illness. Escaping isn't in his words at all.

Yes. The Amalekites were "…eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah." They're spread out and having a party. That's a whole lot of plunder to celebrate.

Sleeping isn't what the text describes, friend. It says the Amalekites were "…eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder…" That's a big spread, and they're enjoying it. Sleeping it off just isn't in the verse.

Packing isn't what the text describes, friend. They're "…spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken…" That's what David finds when the Egyptian leads him there.
Almost, but the text has an exception. David struck them down, "Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels." So some got away. They rode off on camels.

David does say "My brothers" to the men who want to keep the plunder, but he never says anything about family. The reason he gives is, "…you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us." It's about what the LORD gave.

Double, friend? Somebody's negotiating hard! That's not what David says. The share of the one who went to battle "…will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies." Then he adds, "They will share alike."

Priests, friend? Nice try, but that's not the word in the text. David sent the gift to "…his friends, the elders of Judah…" with the message, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies." Elders fills the blank, and I think it's a generous gift.
